rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The women backed Zulaykhā’s ultimatum and told Joseph he must obey or face prison.
rows.anchor: they supported her, telling him that he had no choice but to obey her command, lest he be thrown into prison (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph preferred the Hereafter to fleeting worldly pleasure: illicit surrender meant next-life punishment, while prison meant hardship now and felicity later; human love was real but illicit beside God’s Love.
rows.anchor: he preferred the next life over the fleeting pleasures of this life

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: Joseph turned to God in humility.
rows.anchor: Joseph turned to God in humility (Kl)

rows.speaker: Qu
rows.claim: Joseph sought God’s assistance because only God, rather than his own efforts, could save him.
rows.anchor: he knew that he could only be saved from his plight by God, not as a result of his own efforts (Qu)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: God strengthened Joseph’s resistance to the women so that he accepted prison’s hardships.
rows.anchor: so strengthening his ability to resist the women that he actually accepted the hardships of prison (Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran links supplication with God’s response, as in 40:60.

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: One interpretation takes them to mean Potiphar’s family and Zulaykhā.

rows.speaker: Kl

rows.anchor: the family of Potiphar and Zulaykhā or to those members of Potiphar’s entourage with whom he consulted about this matter (Kl)

rows.speaker: JJ and Kl
rows.claim: The signs were indications of Joseph’s innocence.
rows.anchor: the signs refers to the indications of Joseph’s innocence (JJ, Kl)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Imprisonment was temporary, until rumors about Joseph and Zulaykhā subsided.
rows.anchor: a temporary measure until the rumors about what transpired between Joseph and Zulaykhā had subsided (JJ; cf. Genesis 39:20)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentaries identify the two young men as servants of Egypt’s king.
rows.anchor: Most commentaries state that the two young men who were in prison with Joseph were servants to the king of Egypt.

rows.speaker: Ṭ and JJ
rows.claim: One prisoner was the king’s baker and the other his wine carrier.
rows.anchor: One of them was his baker (Ṭ) and the other his wine carrier (JJ, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R and Ṭ
rows.claim: The baker had plotted to poison the king; the wine carrier was imprisoned as a suspected accomplice.
rows.anchor: since the king thought that he had aided the baker in the attempt to kill him (R,Ṭ;

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: The wine dream belonged to the wine carrier, and the bread dream to the baker.
rows.anchor: dreamed of the wine was the wine carrier, and the young man who had dreamed of the bread was the baker (Bg;

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: They asked Joseph to interpret their dreams because they had seen him interpret others’ dreams.
rows.anchor: because they had seen him interpret other people’s dreams (JJ)

rows.speaker: Al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says they trusted Joseph’s dream interpretation because his virtuous conduct, kindness, and devout practice showed him to be among the virtuous.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī reports that, seeing Joseph’s virtuous character and kind behavior toward the other prison mates

rows.speaker: N and Kl
rows.claim: The wine carrier would survive and regain his former post serving wine to Egypt’s king.
rows.anchor: former position (N) as a wine server to the king of Egypt (Kl;

rows.speaker: My
rows.claim: The baker would be crucified for his crime, and birds would eat from his head after death.
rows.anchor: the baker would be crucified for his crime, and after his death the birds would eat from his head (My;

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: Joseph asked the wine carrier to mention him to Egypt’s king.
rows.anchor: Joseph told the wine carrier to mention him to the king of Egypt (Kl; cf. Genesis 40:14–15)

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: Satan made the wine carrier forget Joseph, prolonging Joseph’s imprisonment.
rows.anchor: Satan caused him to forget to make mention to his lord; that is, he forgot to mention Joseph to the king (Kl)

rows.speaker: IK and N
rows.claim: Most commentators say Joseph remained imprisoned for seven years.
rows.anchor: a total of seven years according to most commentators (IK, N)

rows.speaker: Kl and Q
rows.claim: An alternative translation says Satan made Joseph forget to remember God, meaning Joseph forgot God when asking the carrier to mention him.
rows.anchor: Satan caused him to forget remembering his Lord,” in which case it would mean that at the particular moment when Joseph told the wine carrier

rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Joseph would have been released earlier had he remembered God when asking the wine carrier to mention him.
rows.anchor: According to Ibn ʿAbbās, had Joseph remembered God when he told the wine carrier

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet prayed for Joseph and said his request to be mentioned to the king resulted in a longer imprisonment.

rows.speaker: Kl and JJ
rows.claim: The notables were high-ranking members of the king’s entourage, and he asked them to interpret his dream.
rows.anchor: high offices in his kingdom (Kl), to give him their opinion means that he wanted them to interpret the dream for him (JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Visions here means true or veridical dreams, as discussed at 12:4.
rows.anchor: By visions here are meant true or veridical dreams (see 12:4c).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ʿabara comes from ʿ-b-r, meaning to cross from one side to another; in dream interpretation it describes moving from symbolic dream forms to their actual meanings.
rows.anchor: moving from the imaginal and symbolic forms in dreams to the actual meanings they symbolize (Bḍ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king’s dream is interpreted in 12:47–49.
rows.anchor: For the interpretation of the king’s dream, see vv. 47–49 (cf. Genesis 41:1–8).

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: The wine carrier remembered Joseph’s words from 12:42.
rows.anchor: The wine carrier remembered Joseph’s words in v. 42 (Bg)

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: After a while means seven years, matching Joseph’s imprisonment in 12:42.
rows.anchor: After a while refers to a period of seven years (Bg), which corresponds to the length of time Joseph spent in prison

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wine carrier persuaded the king to consult Joseph by citing Joseph’s earlier accurate dream interpretation.
rows.anchor: by pointing to his own experience with Joseph’s powers of dream interpretation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s interpretation covers the next fifteen years of Egypt’s agricultural cycle.
rows.anchor: what would happen during the next fifteen years of Egypt’s agrarian cycle

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The first seven years would be fertile and abundant, so Egyptians should sow diligently.
rows.anchor: During the first phase, the Egyptians would sow diligently for seven years, as this would be a time of great fertility and abundance (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph advised storing most of the first phase’s harvest so people would have food during the second phase.
rows.anchor: Joseph proposed to store up much of the harvest during the first phase so that the people would have food during the second phase.

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The second phase would be seven extremely difficult years of dearth.
rows.anchor: The second phase would bring seven hard [years], that is, a time of dearth that would be exceedingly difficult for people (R)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The final year would bring abundant bounty; pressing oil and wine signaled that food was plentiful again.
rows.anchor: the pressing of oil and wine is an indication that there would be food in abundance once again; cf. Genesis 41:25–36.

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: After hearing Joseph’s interpretation, the king asked the messenger to bring Joseph to him.
rows.anchor: the king asked that he bring Joseph to him (JJ)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Joseph sought to clear himself by asking the king to confront the women who had cut their hands.
rows.anchor: which is understood to have been Joseph’s request that the women be confronted by the king (JJ)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The messenger conveyed Joseph’s inquiry, and the king gathered the women.
rows.anchor: the king complied by gathering the women before him (JJ)

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: The women’s denial of knowing evil against Joseph absolved him of blame.
rows.anchor: the women said they did not know of any evil against him, which is to say that they absolved Joseph of any blame (Kl)

rows.speaker: My
rows.claim: Some commentators say Zulaykhā’s love had surpassed self-interest, leading her to tell the truth about Joseph.
rows.anchor: her love for Joseph had grown so strong that it had surpassed her own self-interest, and so she spoke the truth about him (My)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier Zulaykhā falsely blamed Joseph because her desire mattered more to her than his well-being.
rows.anchor: Before, she had blamed him for a sin he did not commit, because her own desire was more important than his well-being (see v. 25).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Later she admitted his innocence only to a small group of women to protect herself from their scorn.
rows.anchor: Later, she admitted Joseph’s innocence, but only to a small group of women as a way of absolving herself of scorn in their eyes (see v. 32).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative presents Zulaykhā’s spiritual development as a progression from sensual attraction to love that recognizes Joseph’s inward beauty.
rows.anchor: the narrative indicates that there was a progression in the degrees of love in Zulaykhā’s own soul and therefore in her spiritual journey

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Her spiritual love for Joseph’s inward beauty parallels Potiphar’s earlier recognition of it in the marketplace.
rows.anchor: much like Potiphar did when he first saw him in the marketplace (see 12:21–22c)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s inner virtue, especially truthfulness, catalyzed this change, and Zulaykhā recognized it in calling him truthful.
rows.anchor: Joseph’s inner virtues, marked by his quality of truthfulness, which Zulaykhā recognized when she referred to him as among the truthful

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: Joseph’s question recalls the brothers’ separation of him from Benjamin in youth, their harm to Joseph, and their injustices toward Benjamin, including insults and degradation.
rows.anchor: harming him (Joseph) and perpetrating injustices against Benjamin, such as debasing and reviling him (Kl)

rows.speaker: Kl and R
rows.claim: One explanation of when you were ignorant is that they did not understand how vile their actions were.
rows.anchor: their ignorance of the vileness of their actions or their general state of ignorance on account of their youth (Kl)

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: An alternative explanation is that the brothers were generally ignorant because of their youth.
rows.anchor: their general state of ignorance on account of their youth (Kl)

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: One report says the brothers recognized Joseph when he spoke these words, or when he smiled.
rows.anchor: that the brothers recognized that their interlocutor was Joseph when he spoke these words to them, or when he smiled (Bḍ)

rows.speaker: Sh
rows.claim: Another report says the brothers recognized Joseph when he removed his crown.
rows.anchor: or when he removed his crown (Sh)

rows.speaker: author

rows.anchor: For Surely God neglects not the reward of the virtuous, see 9:120; 11:11c, 115c; 12:56.

rows.speaker: My
rows.claim: Jacob addressed the members of his tribe who were with him.
rows.anchor: Jacob’s words were addressed to those of his tribe who were with him (My)

rows.speaker: Bg and My
rows.claim: Jacob sensed Joseph because the heavenly scent from Joseph’s shirt reached him as the caravan traveled from Egypt to Canaan.
rows.anchor: Jacob was able to perceive Joseph’s scent because of the heavenly smell that came from his shirt (Bg, My)

rows.speaker: My
rows.claim: Some say Jacob’s perception was a miracle because both Jacob and Joseph were prophets.
rows.anchor: Some say that this was a miracle because Jacob and Joseph were prophets (My)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah Ibrāhīm is the fifth of six sūrahs beginning with alif, lām, rāʾ and speaking of the Book.
rows.anchor: verses include the letters alif, lām, and rāʾ, and which speak of

rows.claim: It is said to be Makkan except verses 28–29, which are Madinan and usually understood to refer to Badr.
rows.anchor: which belong to the Madinan period, as these two verses are usually considered to refer to the Battle of Badr (My)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah takes its name from Abraham’s episode and prayer, which asks security for Makkah, protection from idolatry for himself and his children, and prosperity for his progeny.
rows.anchor: the security of Makkah, protection from idolatry for himself and his children, prosperity for his progeny

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham also prayed for forgiveness for his parents and all believers on the Last Day.
rows.anchor: forgiveness for his parents and all believers on the Last Day.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A key theme is the sharp difference between gratitude and ingratitude for God’s blessings.
rows.anchor: gratitude and ingratitude for God’s Blessings (see vv. 5, 7–8, 28, 32–34, 37)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah stresses patience and trust in God.
rows.anchor: importance of patience (vv. 5, 12) and trust in God (vv. 11–12)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another theme is the terrible nature of divine chastisement in this world and the next.
rows.anchor: whether in this world or in the next (vv. 16–17,29–31, 42–44, 48–50)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who prefer worldly life to the Hereafter lose in the next life; rejectors of messengers are one example.
rows.anchor: those who prefer the life of this world over the Hereafter will end up as losers in the next life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rejecting God’s messengers is one form of preferring this world over the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: those who reject God’s messengers (vv. 3, 9–10, 28–30)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ingratitude for God’s many blessings typifies those who lose in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: are ungrateful to God for the many blessings that He has given to them (vv. 17–18)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking partners alongside God is another such example.
rows.anchor: take partners alongside God (v. 30)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Succumbing to Satan’s false promises is another such example.
rows.anchor: succumb to Satan’s false promises (v. 22)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophecy guides people out of darkness into light.
rows.anchor: prophecy as a means of guiding people out of darkness into light (vv. 1, 5)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether people are guided ultimately lies in God’s hands.
rows.anchor: whether they are guided or not is ultimately in God’s Hands (vv. 4, 21, 27, 37)
